turns.t: Doctor, I'm Meena, I look after Mrs Rao in the daytime. Her fingers go white, very white, in the cold. She wanted me here.
Yes. White.
When does it happen, Mrs Rao?
Cold. Fridge. Winter.
Even when she takes the milk out of the fridge, doctor. And the tips of the fingers go blue after, and then red.
Is it painful?
When warm. Tingling. Pain.
It's worse in the evening, she rubs her hands together and she cries a little.
Any sores on the fingertips?
No sores.
What do you take at the moment?
Nifedipine. Ten. Two times.
Nifedipine, 10 mg, twice a day, doctor, that's what it says on the box.
Good. Is it helping? ~
Little. ~
A little, yes. She's not been wearing the gloves. ~
Let me check you. Blood pressure 118 over 72, pulse 78.
Fine? ~
Fine. Let me see your hands. Hold them out.
Show the doctor. ~
Here. ~
Your fingertips are pale and cool compared to the rest of your hand.
That's how they look in the clinic, too. ~
Now I'll explain. Raynaud's is when the small blood vessels in the fingers squeeze too tightly in the cold. ~
Squeeze. Yes. ~
It can be on its own, but sometimes it's linked to another condition, like an autoimmune one, and I can't rule that out yet.
Is it dangerous? ~
Not on its own. But I'd like to keep an eye on it. Keep her hands warm, wear gloves, and avoid smoking and caffeine.
She doesn't smoke. She drinks a lot of tea. ~
Maybe cut it to a few cups. ~
Okay. ~
Should she wear the gloves at night, too? ~
Thin cotton ones can help, yes. ~
I'll make sure. ~
Mrs Rao, do you understand what I've said? ~
Yes. Gloves. Warm. ~
Exactly. I'd like to see you again in six weeks.
Six weeks. I'll bring her. ~
